slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter twenty-five: the examination of nirvana.

slides.heading: Is nirvana a destination?
points: Suffering now, freedom later
A calm place, reached when life's noise is left behind?
What could nirvana be, if everything is empty?
slides.say: Every spiritual path seems to promise a destination. Suffering now, freedom later; this world now, a better state beyond it. The Buddhist word for that freedom is nirvana, blowing out, and it is easy to picture it as somewhere to arrive: a calm place reached when the noise of life has been left behind. This chapter asks what nirvana could be, if everything examined so far has turned out to be empty.

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: Nirvana as a thing, an absence, both or neither?
Not the slightest difference from the round of births
What goes is the picture of a second world
slides.say: It comes straight after the great defence of emptiness in chapter twenty-four. Here Nagarjuna turns to the goal itself. He tests every way of taking nirvana as a thing, an absence, both or neither, and then says the most startling sentence in the whole work: there is not the slightest difference between nirvana and the round of birth and death. As in chapter one, nothing that works is taken away. What goes is the picture of a second world.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
The Sanskrit is shown above each verse
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Emptiness leaves nothing to end?
slides.say: Now the explanation. The chapter opens with the opponent. Freedom, says the tradition, comes from abandoning the afflictions, greed, hatred and confusion, and from the ceasing of the aggregates. But if everything is empty, nothing really arises and nothing really passes away. Then there is nothing to abandon and nothing to cease. Nagarjuna answers with the same words turned round. Suppose things are not empty. Then each affliction has a nature of its own, fixed from its own side. A thing like that cannot arise from conditions, and it cannot be ended by changing conditions either. Anger with its own nature would simply be anger, for ever. So it is the opponent's view, not emptiness, that leaves nothing to abandon. Then comes the definition: nirvana is not abandoned and not attained, not cut off and not permanent, not ceased and not arisen. These are the same kinds of negation as the homage in chapter one: they remove the picture of a thing with whereabouts, not the freedom itself.

slides.heading: Is nirvana a thing?
points: It would age and die, like every thing we know
It would be conditioned, one more product of causes
It would depend, and could be taken away again
slides.say: The next verses test the first option: nirvana as an existing thing, something real in its own right. Three problems follow at once. It would age and die, because everything we know as an existing thing is marked by coming to be and passing away. It would be conditioned, one more house built on sand. And it would depend: a nirvana that depended on causes could be taken away again when they changed.

slides.heading: An absence, both, or neither?
points: An absence is always the absence of something
The round no longer going on, driven by grasping
Both: something and nothing at once. Neither: built from both
slides.say: Perhaps then nirvana is an absence, the mere ending of suffering, as a flame is simply gone? But an absence is always the absence of something. No milk in the jug only makes sense against milk. So an absence, too, is dependent. Verse twenty-five point nine gives the key. Birth and death come and go in dependence, through conditions: that is samsara. When this coming and going no longer runs on in dependence and through conditions, that is called nirvana. Chandrakirti glosses it simply as the round no longer going on. What stops is a round driven by grasping, and nothing else needs to be added. The Buddha told us to abandon craving for becoming and for non-becoming, so nirvana is neither a thing nor an absence. Could it be both? Then liberation would be both something and nothing, like light and darkness in the same spot. And neither a thing nor an absence is a phrase built out of thing and absence; it makes sense only if those two had already been established.

slides.heading: The four corners
slides.say: These are the four corners of the chapter's test: a thing, an absence, both, and neither. As in chapter one, refusing all four is not a fifth theory of nirvana. It removes the assumption that nirvana is something to be located. The same holds for the old unanswered questions. Asked whether the Buddha exists after death, does not exist, both or neither, the Buddha set the question aside. Nagarjuna presses the point, as the Buddha himself did with the monk Anuradha: the same four answers fail even while the Buddha is alive. The question was never about what happens at death. It was about whether there is a Buddha found from his own side, a self to exist or not exist. There never was, before death or after. So the silence was not a secret held back. There was nothing for any of the four answers to be about.

slides.heading: Not the slightest difference
slides.say: Now the verses that have been quoted ever since, twenty-five point nineteen and twenty. There is nothing that sets samsara apart from nirvana, and nothing that sets nirvana apart from samsara. Between the limit of the one and the limit of the other, not even the finest gap is found. It is important to read this exactly. It does not say that suffering is liberation, or that a confused, grasping life is already free. It says that samsara and nirvana are not two places, two kinds of stuff, or two worlds. Look for the edge you would cross to get from one to the other. No such edge is found, because neither side is found standing on its own. So there is still a difference, but not where we looked for it. It is a difference in how the same appearance is met: grasped as solid things, with all the fear and craving that brings, or seen through, and let be. In nature they are equally empty; in convention one is bondage and the other freedom, and the path is the removal of a misreading.

slides.heading: Where views come from
points: The Buddha after death rests on nirvana as a place
An end rests on the later limit; permanence on the earlier
All things are empty: what is there to end or last?
slides.say: Verses twenty-one to twenty-three explain why people keep asking the unanswerable questions. Each set of views rests on something taken as a fixed point. Views about the Buddha after death rest on nirvana, pictured as a final place. Views about an end rest on the later limit, the future. Views about permanence rest on the earlier limit, the past. Each view takes for granted something with a nature of its own, which could last or not last, end or not end. But all things are empty. Then what is there to be endless or to have an end, permanent or impermanent? The questions are not hard. They have nothing to be about. Chapter twenty-seven takes these views apart one by one.

slides.heading: No teaching, taught to no one
points: The quieting of all taking-as-objects
The quieting of elaborations, peace: the homage again
Taught for forty-five years; no teaching found from its own side
slides.say: The chapter ends with peace. Nirvana is the quieting of all taking-as-objects and the quieting of elaborations. Taking-as-object is the grip that turns each appearance into a thing to hold. When that grip relaxes, the spinning of is and is not stops by itself. The words the quieting of elaborations, peace, are the same words used in the homage of chapter one. The text has come round to its opening. Then a line that sounds like a paradox: the Buddha never taught any teaching to anyone, anywhere. Of course he taught for forty-five years. But no teaching existed from its own side, no listener was found as a self, and no place held the event. The teaching worked, as a raft works for crossing a river, because it was empty.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: Suffering, coming from conditions, can end
The difference between a grasping mind and a free one
Removed: nirvana as a place elsewhere
slides.say: Read quickly, this chapter seems to empty the path of its goal. It does the opposite. It shows why a goal is possible at all: suffering, coming from conditions, can end when its conditions end. It keeps the difference between a grasping mind and a free one, which is the whole difference that matters. It keeps the path, the practice and the teacher, each working as designated. What it removes is the picture of nirvana as a place elsewhere, reached by leaving this world behind.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: Notice a moment of irritation
Look for its own nature, its edge
Seen that way, it loosens: this world, no longer misread
slides.say: The test is close at hand. Notice a moment of irritation. Look for where it stands, its own nature, its edge. It is vivid, and it is not found apart from its conditions: the remark, the tiredness, the story told about it. Seen that way, it loosens. Nothing has gone anywhere, and nothing new has arrived. This is how the chapter can say that nirvana is not a second world: it is this world, no longer misread.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: the Interlude, 'Nirvana'
Anatta to Emptiness: Resonances and Open Questions
The Appendix: conventional and nirvanic states
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World, the Interlude's section on nirvana reads it as this world no longer misread, citing verses twenty-five point nineteen to twenty and twenty-five point twenty-four. In The Transition from Anatta to Emptiness, Resonances and Open Questions takes up the shared limit, and the difference between sharing nirvana's nature and having realised it; and the Appendix restates the shared limit in the book's notation. Two talks on YouTube take it up too. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter twenty-six, the examination of the twelve links.
